extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX Coordinators, compliance officers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX nondisclosure and informal resolution
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance and regulatory text interpreting 34 CFR §106.44(j) (nondisclosure of personally identifiable information) and §106.44(k) (informal resolution): explains the scope of nondisclosure protections, five enumerated exceptions, interplay with FERPA and other laws, and the limits, timing, and required safeguards for informal resolution processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of nondisclosure — personally identifiable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j) prohibits disclosure of any 'personally identifiable information' obtained by a recipient in the course of complying with this part; 'personally identifiable information' is information that would tend to reveal the identity of an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers PII obtained while fulfilling Title IX obligations (e.g., supportive measures, requests for pregnancy-related reasonable modifications, information about complainants/respondents/witnesses/other participants). The Department adopted the broader term 'personally identifiable information' instead of 'identity' to protect not just names but any information that would tend to reveal identity. Unauthorized disclosures can chill reporting and lead to harassment, retaliation, or other sex-based harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondisclosure prohibition cannot be used for retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when an exception to the nondisclosure prohibition applies, a disclosure cannot be made for retaliatory purposes per §106.71.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must ensure disclosures are not motivated by retaliation; e.g., a disclosure under an exception that has the purpose of harassing or retaliating against the student is prohibited. Recipients should assess intent and purpose before disclosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception 1 — Prior written consent from person with legal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(1) permits disclosure when the recipient has obtained prior written consent to the disclosure 'from a person with the legal right to consent to the disclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must obtain consent from whoever has legal authority under applicable Federal or State law (e.g., parents for minors in elementary/secondary schools under FERPA). If that person is not the subject of the PII, the recipient need not also obtain consent from the subject. If the PII is in an education record, FERPA consent rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception 2 — Disclosures to parents/guardians/authorized legal representatives with legal right
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(2) clarifies that the nondisclosure paragraph does not prohibit disclosures to a parent, guardian, or other authorized legal representative who has the legal right to receive disclosures on behalf of the person whose PII is at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception is intended to permit application of legal rights conferred by FERPA and State law. Example: parents of minors in elementary/secondary schools generally have FERPA rights to inspect education records; postsecondary 'eligible students' may limit parental access absent consent or FERPA exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception 3 — Disclosures to carry out Title IX regulations/purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(3) permits disclosures 'to carry out the purposes of the Department's Title IX regulations, including action taken to address conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination' under the part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures necessary to implement supportive measures (limited to what is necessary), to provide parties access to evidence per §§106.45(f)(4) and 106.46(e)(6), or to implement §§106.44, 106.45, or 106.46 are allowed. Example: informing a professor that a student is receiving a supportive measure but disclosing only information necessary to implement it. Recipients must avoid disclosures that would conflict with FERPA (presence of third persons must not lead to FERPA-conflicting disclosures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception 4 — Disclosures required by Federal law, regulations, or terms/conditions of a Federal award
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(4) permits disclosures required by Federal law, Federal regulations, or the terms and conditions of a Federal award (including grants or other funding agreements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may disclose when compelled by federal statute/regulation or grant terms, but such disclosures must also comply with FERPA and other applicable Federal law. The Department added 'Federal regulations' language to address interactions with FERPA, HIPAA, and their implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception 5 — Disclosures permitted or required by FERPA or State/local law to extent not conflicting with Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j)(5) permits disclosures that are permitted (but not required) under FERPA, and disclosures required by State or local law, to the extent such disclosures do not conflict with Title IX or the Department's regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where FERPA or state law would permit/require disclosure, the recipient must not make disclosures that would, for example, create sex-based discrimination, chill reporting, be retaliatory, harassing, or otherwise hinder the recipient's ability to operate free from sex discrimination. State or local laws that conflict with Title IX are preempted by §106.6(b). Example: mandatory reporting about an employee accused of sexually assaulting a student may be permitted if it does not conflict with Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to ensure compliance with FERPA and other Federal laws when disclosing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must ensure that any permitted disclosure complies with FERPA or any other applicable Federal laws and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When PII is part of an education record, FERPA consent/exception rules apply; recipients must evaluate whether a proposed disclosure is consistent with FERPA and Title IX (and other federal requirements such as HIPAA), and cannot rely on a federal award term that would conflict with FERPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disclosures that create a hostile environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of personally identifiable information that creates a 'hostile environment' as defined under §106.2 would be prohibited under these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations are case-by-case. Example: broadly disclosing a student's sexual orientation or gender identity in a way that results in sex-based harassment would likely be prohibited. Recipients should assess foreseeable sex-based harms from a disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology choice — protect more than 'identity'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adopted the more comprehensive term 'personally identifiable information' instead of the proposed term 'identity' because 'identity' might be interpreted to protect only a name rather than information that reveals identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the broader 'personally identifiable information' understanding (any information that would tend to reveal identity) when assessing confidentiality obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures confidentiality — limit to necessary information
rubrics_metrics.description: When notifying others (e.g., professors) about supportive measures, recipients may disclose only personally identifiable information that is necessary to implement the supportive measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disclose PII about related complaints or allegations beyond what is necessary for implementation. See §106.44(g)(5) discussion for more on nondisclosure protections regarding supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution — voluntariness, informed consent, and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Section §106.44(k) requires informal resolution to be voluntary and informed, and any person facilitating informal resolutions must be 'appropriately trained' under §106.8(d)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained training and independence expectations equivalent to those for formal grievance facilitators. 'Informal resolution' is understood as 'alternative dispute resolution' and can encompass many conflict resolution strategies; being 'informal' does not mean less rigorous training or lesser seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and right to withdraw from informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may offer informal resolution 'at any time before determining whether sex discrimination occurred,' including before an investigation begins or during an investigation; any party retains the right to withdraw from informal resolution prior to agreeing to a resolution and to initiate or resume the recipient's grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may not require a formal complaint or completed investigation before offering informal resolution. If a party withdraws, grievance procedures must be available. If parties pursue informal resolution without a complaint, §106.44(k)(3)(iii) safeguards rescindability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on availability of informal resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must not offer informal resolution in two situations: (1) when there are allegations that an employee engaged in sex-based harassment of an elementary or secondary school student, and (2) when an informal resolution would conflict with applicable Federal, State, or local law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond those two mandatory prohibitions, the recipient has discretion to decline informal resolution (e.g., evidence of coercion, ongoing threat to others, or other circumstances making informal resolution inappropriate). The recipient should consider factors enumerated in §106.44(f)(1)(v)(A) when deciding whether to initiate informal resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and enforceability of informal resolution agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential terms of informal resolution agreements may include (but are not limited to) restrictions on contact, restrictions on respondent participation in programs or events, and restrictions similar to remedies or disciplinary sanctions; agreements can be voided by the recipient for breach, fraud, or other compelling reasons, in which case grievance procedures may be initiated or resumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.44(k)(5) explicitly allows such terms. Recipient must exercise discretion equitably and may void agreements if breached or procured by fraud. An admission in informal resolution does not by itself constitute a determination that sex discrimination occurred under §106.45/§106.46.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution not appropriate for structural complaints (complaints against recipient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal resolution is not available for complaints that allege a recipient's policy or practice discriminates on the basis of sex (i.e., structural complaints) because such complaints are against the recipient itself rather than a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon notification of a potentially discriminatory policy or practice, the recipient may address the matter under §106.44(f)(1) prompt-and-effective response obligations (including 'other appropriate prompt and effective steps') rather than informal resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator obligations re: notice of options
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.44(f)(1)(iii)(A) and related provisions, the Title IX Coordinator must notify the complainant (or the reporter if complainant unknown) of the grievance procedures (§106.45 and if applicable §106.46) and the informal resolution process (§106.44(k)), if available and appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Coordinator is not required to initiate grievance procedures for every report; notification of available processes is required. The Coordinator may delegate duties but must ensure parties are informed of options.
